The first recorded travels by Europeans to China and back date from this time. The most famous traveler of the period was the Venetian Marco Polo, whose account of his trip to "Cambaluc," the capital of the Great Khan, and of life there astounded the people of Europe. The account of his travels, Il milione (or, The Million, known in English as the Travels of Marco Polo), appeared about the year 1299. Some argue over the accuracy of Marco Polo's accounts due to the lack of mentioning the Great Wall of China, tea houses, which would have been a prominent sight since Europeans had yet to adopt a tea culture, as well the practice of foot binding by the women in capital of the Great Khan. Some suggest that Marco Polo acquired much of his knowledge through contact with Persian traders since many of the places he named were in Persian.

How did some suspect that Polo learned about China instead of by actually visiting it?

Answer: through contact with Persian traders

## Entire corpus

## What is a language model?

Language model: A probabilistic model of a sequence of words

Formal definition:

A language model computes the joint probability:  $ P(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)}) $

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_288_855_1213_1386.jpg" alt="Image" width="34%" /></div>


"The cat sits on the mat."

"The dog runs in the park."

"I like machine learning."

Meaning of  $ \mathrm{P}(w^{(1)}, w^{(2)}, \ldots, w^{(t)}) $ :

How likely is this sequence of words to appear in real-world language use?

<!-- page: 7 -->

## Chain rule

The probability of a sentence can be decomposed into a product of next-word probabilities.

 $$ \begin{array}{r l}{\mathbf{\nabla\Phi P\left(w^{(1)},w^{(2)},\ldots,w^{(t)}\right)}=}&{{}}\\ {\mathbf{\nabla\Phi P\left(w^{(1)}\right)}\times}&{{}\mathbf{P}\left(w^{(2)}|w^{(1)}\right)\times\cdots\times\mathbf{P}\left(w^{(t)}\mid w^{(1)},w^{(2)},\ldots,w^{(t-1)}\right)}\\ &{{}\mathrm{C o n d i t i o n a l~p r o b a b i l i t y}}\end{array} $$ 

Concrete example:

Sentence: “The dog runs in the park.”

P(The dog runs in the park.) = P(The) * P(dog | the) * P(runs | The dog)

 $$ ^{*}P(\mathrm{i n}\mid\mathrm{T h e~d o g~r u n s})*P(\mathrm{t h e}\mid\mathrm{T h e~d o g~r u n s~i n}) $$ 

 $ ^{*} $P(park | The dog runs in the)

<!-- page: 8 -->

## Next word prediction

Given the previous words, predict the probability of the next word.

 $$ P(w^{(t)}|w^{(1)},w^{(2)},\ldots,w^{(t-1)}) $$ 

Select or sample one word, append it to the context, and repeat.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_926_722_1997_1018.jpg" alt="Image" width="40%" /></div>


Almost all tasks can be framed as predicting the next word:

Translation: “Hello in Chinese is”  $ \rightarrow $ “你好”

Coding: "def add(a, b): return"  $ \rightarrow $ a + b

QA: "The first man on the moon was"  $ \rightarrow $ Neil

Sentiment: "I hated this movie. Sentiment:" → Negative

## How do we represent the meaning of a word?

## Intuition

Different words should have different representations.

Related words should have similar representations.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_796_853_1954_1499.jpg" alt="Image" width="43%" /></div>

<!-- page: 11 -->

## One-hot representation

Different words should have different vectors

Assign each word a unique sparse vector.

Vocabulary table: [cat, dog, car, apple, run]

cat => [1,0,0,0,0]

dog => [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]

car => [0, 0, 1, 0, 0]

apple => [0, 0, 0, 1, 0]

run => [0, 0, 0, 0, 1]

Q: What are the issues with representing a word this way?

A: All words are equally (dis)similar; e.g., the dot products for (cat, dog) and (cat, car) are both zero

## Problems with fully connected language models

Bag-of-Words only counts word occurrences

Different sentences may have the same bag-of-words vector

cat => [1, 0, 0, 0, 0]

chase => [0, 1, 0, 0, 0]

dog => [0,0,1,0,0]

“cat chase dog” => [1, 1, 1, 0, 0]

“dog chase cat” => [I, I, I, 0, 0]

Same words, same BoW vector, but different meanings.

The fully connected network predicts from a bag of words, not from an ordered sequence representation.

## Limitations of recurrent language models

Learning bottleneck: Information decay

■ All previous tokens are compressed into $h_{t}$.

Information from $x_{i}$ must pass through many updates to affect $h_{t}$.

System inefficiency

■ Sequential computation: $h_{t}$ depends on $h_{t-1}$.

Training/serving large models becomes cost-prohibitive due to time constraints.

## Attention as a soft, weighted lookup table

In attention, the query softly matches each key,

producing a weight between 0 and 1. The keys' values

are multiplied by the weights and summed.

In a lookup table, we have a table of keys that map

to values. The query matches one of the keys,

returning its value.

## A closer look

## Matrix form

 $$  Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax(QK^{T}/\sqrt{d_{k}}+M)V $$ 

Each row compares one query with every key. Apply softmax across that row.

## Causal self-attention

M adds 0 to allowed scores and  $ -\infty $ to future scores before softmax.

For “Thinking,” masking “Machines” changes the weights from [0.88, 0.12] to [1, 0].

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_chart_box_1782_406_2494_1033.jpg" alt="Image" width="26%" /></div>


Scores before softmax. Gray cells are masked.

Doubling the sequence length gives four times as many cells in the full score grid.

<!-- page: 47 -->

$$  Head=Attention(Q,K,V)=softmax\left(\frac{QK^{T}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V $$ 

## Multi-head attention

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_147_405_894_1323.jpg" alt="Image" width="28%" /></div>


<div style="text-align: center;">Each head has its own Q, K and V projections.</div>


## How is it computed?

Multi-head Attention $(Q,K,V)=concat(head_{1},head_{2},...,head_{h})W^{O}$

## Why does it work?

Different heads learn different attention patterns

Heads can capture multiple relations simultaneously, e.g., local context, long-range dependencies, and syntactic/semantic links

■ Concatenation aggregates diverse information into a richer token representation

With $d = 512$ and $h = 8$ heads, each key has $d_{k} = 64$ features. Scale each head's scores by dividing by $\sqrt{64} = 8$.

Weighted output at “bites”

 $$ 0.50\mathrm{v_{dog}}+0.20\mathrm{v_{bites}}+0.30\mathrm{v_{man}} $$ 

 $$ 0.30\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{m a n}}+0.20\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{b i t e s}}+0.50\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{d o g}} $$ 

Each word keeps its key, value and weight, so both rows give the same sum.

<!-- page: 52 -->

## Positional embeddings

■ Sinusoidal positional representations concatenate sinusoidal functions with varying periods.

 $$ \widetilde{x}_{i}=x_{i}+p_{i} $$ 

 $$ \begin{array}{r l}{\pmb{p}_{i}=}&{\left(\begin{matrix}{\sin(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\ {\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\ {\vdots}\\ {\sin(i/|10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\\ {\cos(i/10000^{2*\frac{d}{2}/d})}\end{matrix}\right)}\end{array} $$ 

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_chart_box_1060_709_2547_1138.jpg" alt="Image" width="55%" /></div>


Index in the sequence

<!-- page: 53 -->

## Adding nonlinearities after self-attention

• Self-attention has no elementwise nonlinear activation on its outputs. Stacking attention layers keeps re-averaging value vectors.

• Add a feed-forward network after self-attention. Its activation function, such as ReLU, introduces elementwise nonlinearity.

 $$ m_{i}\;=\;W_{2}\operatorname{R e L U}(W_{1}\;o_{i}\;+\;b_{1})\;+\;b_{2} $$ 

o: attention output at position i

Softmax sets attention weights. ReLU adds a nonlinear transformation of the output features.

<div style="text-align: center;"><img src="imgs/img_in_image_box_1467_406_2510_1392.jpg" alt="Image" width="39%" /></div>


Each layer shares its FFN weights across token positions.

<!-- page: 54 -->

## The Transformer Encoder-Decoder

## Encoder inputs

The source is “昨天安娜离开了北京”. Each position can use context on both sides.

## Masked self-attention

To predict “Beijing,” the decoder can read the English prefix “Anna left.”

The decoder supplies the query. Encoder states for the Chinese input supply the keys and values.

## GPT-I (2018)

GPT (2018) was a major success in decoder pretraining.

Transformer decoder with 12 layers, 117M parameters.

768-dimensional hidden states, 3072-dimensional feed-forward hidden layers.

Byte-pair encoding with 40,000 merges

■ Trained on BookCorpus: over 7,000 unique books.

It contains long spans of contiguous text for learning long-distance dependencies.

## GPT-3, In-context learning, and very large models (2020)

Very large language models seem to perform some kind of learning without gradient steps simply from examples you provide within their context windows. The in-context examples seem to specify the task to be performed, and the conditional distribution mimics performing the task to a certain extent.

## Scaling curse

Compute. Llama 3 405B is trained on up to 16K H100 GPUs, each running at 700W TDP with 80GB HBM3, using Meta’s Grand Teton AI server platform (Matt Bowman, 2022). Each server is equipped with eight GPUs and two CPUs. Within a server, the eight GPUs are connected via NVLink. Training jobs are scheduled using MAST (Choudhury et al., 2024), Meta’s global-scale training scheduler.
